Projects, MSBuild and the dotnet CLI

This content was generated with the assistance of AI and should be verified against the official documentation before being relied on in production.

The reference material consulted while preparing these pages is listed in the section bibliography.

This page is written against Visual Basic 17.13 on .NET 10 (SDK 10.0.402, vbc compiler version 5.9.0-1.26505.111) and was checked on 2026-10-19. Everything marked "built and run" was produced in the .NET 10 SDK container (Linux, arm64) with the real dotnet and vbc commands; the output shown is the output printed. Compiler and MSBuild messages are quoted as printed, so root namespaces and paths in them (/w/...) come from the scratch projects. Project examples are small console programs that start with Option Strict On, or are project files with no code at all. Anything that needs Windows is labelled "built, not run" or "evaluated only". Properties and options are listed by their real names, and the lists were checked against the files the SDK ships (the VB .props and .targets files, Microsoft.VisualBasic.Core.targets and the output of vbc -help).

The project file is where almost every compiler setting in a Visual Basic program lives, and the VB defaults differ from the C# defaults in ways that matter: the SDK ships OptionStrict as Off and a NoWarn list that hides the Option Strict warnings, and several properties known from C# do nothing. Reading this page you will learn what a modern .vbproj contains, how each property becomes a vbc option (all of them, by name), which properties are shared with C# and which exist only for VB, how to set the language version, imports, conditional-compilation symbols and warning policy, how to share settings across a solution, how the dotnet command line drives the same machinery, how Visual Studio’s property pages map onto it, and how the legacy (non-SDK) project format differs. The language-level meaning of Option Strict and its siblings is on Option Statements, the #If directive and symbols on Conditional Compilation and Directives, the My types on The My Namespace, and packaging and publish modes on Libraries, Packaging and Deployment.

The SDK-style project file

A Visual Basic project today is an SDK-style project: a short XML file whose root element names an SDK (Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk"). The SDK supplies, through imported .props and .targets files, everything a project used to list by hand: the source files (a glob), the references to the framework, the default imports, the compiler settings and the build targets. This is what dotnet new writes for the three most common project types (the sources are in the next sections; the listing shows the project files exactly as the templates wrote them):

<!-- dotnet new classlib -lang VB -o Shelf.Core -->
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <RootNamespace>Shelf.Core</RootNamespace>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
  </PropertyGroup>

</Project>

<!-- dotnet new console -lang VB -o Shelf.Cli, then: dotnet add Shelf.Cli reference Shelf.Core -->
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <ItemGroup>
    <ProjectReference Include="..\Shelf.Core\Shelf.Core.vbproj" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <RootNamespace>Shelf.Cli</RootNamespace>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
  </PropertyGroup>

</Project>

<!-- dotnet new mstest -lang VB -o Shelf.Tests -->
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <LangVersion>latest</LangVersion>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="MSTest" Version="4.0.2" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <Using Include="Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>

Three things stand out. A library has no OutputType (the default is Library), a console application has OutputType Exe, and RootNamespace is written into Visual Basic templates (C# templates have no such property, see the next table). The test template carries LangVersion latest (harmless: it means the newest version) and three C#-isms, ImplicitUsings, Nullable and a Using item, that have no effect in a Visual Basic project: the captured vbc command lines in this page do not change when they are set (see Properties that do nothing in Visual Basic). The test template’s own sources and the way the tests run are on Testing.

The project name matters more in VB than in C#, because three names are derived from it and they are independent:

Property Controls Default

AssemblyName

The file name of the output (Shelf.Core.dll) and the assembly identity.

The project file name without extension.

RootNamespace

The namespace the compiler prefixes to every Namespace block and to types declared outside one (/rootnamespace). It also appears in CLR exception messages and in the name of embedded resources and My types.

The project file name, with characters that are not valid in an identifier replaced.

PackageId

The NuGet package id (see Libraries, Packaging and Deployment).

AssemblyName.

What the SDK adds to your project

The following are not in the project file above, but are in force for every Microsoft.NET.Sdk Visual Basic project. Each was observed with dotnet msbuild -getProperty / -getItem, or in the captured command line below.

Implicit What it is

Source files

Compile Include="**/*.vb", minus bin, obj and other default excludes; switched off by EnableDefaultCompileItems = false. **/*.resx become EmbeddedResource items, everything else is None. Putting a file into the folder is enough; listing it again is an error (NETSDK1022, shown below).

Framework reference

The Microsoft.NETCore.App reference pack for the target framework: 167 reference assemblies (for net10.0 on this SDK) passed as /reference:, plus /nostdlib /nosdkpath so the compiler never looks anywhere else.

Visual Basic runtime

Microsoft.VisualBasic.dll (which type-forwards to Microsoft.VisualBasic.Core) passed as /vbruntime:<path>, so Left, Mid, CInt, Format, Like and the My machinery are available without a Reference.

Global imports

/imports:Microsoft.VisualBasic,System,System.Collections,System.Collections.Generic,System.Diagnostics,System.Linq,System.Xml.Linq,System.Threading.Tasks (System.Data is added on .NET Framework targets).

Option defaults

OptionStrict Off, OptionExplicit On, OptionInfer On, OptionCompare Binary.

Warning defaults

NoWarn = 41999,42016,42017,42018,42019,42020,42021,42022,42032,42036 (plus BC41997 added on .NET targets), WarningLevel 1, and WarningsAsErrors NU1605;SYSLIB0011.

Conditional symbols

CONFIG, DEBUG, TRACE, PLATFORM, _MyType, and the target framework symbols (NET, NET10_0, NETCOREAPP, …​); see DefineConstants and the implicit symbols.

Generated source

obj/<config>/<tfm>/<name>.AssemblyInfo.vb (assembly attributes from Version, Company and friends, when GenerateAssemblyInfo is true) and obj/.../.NETCoreApp,Version=v10.0.AssemblyAttributes.vb (the TargetFramework attribute).

Analyzers

The .NET analyzers (Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.VisualBasic.NetAnalyzers.dll and Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.NetAnalyzers.dll) and a global analyzer config for AnalysisLevel.

Where does it come from? The Sdk attribute makes MSBuild import Sdk.props before the project body and Sdk.targets after it. The VB-specific pieces are two small files in the SDK’s Sdks/Microsoft.NET.Sdk/targets folder, selected by the project extension:

File (under the SDK folder) Contents

Sdks/Microsoft.NET.Sdk/targets/Microsoft.NET.Sdk.VisualBasic.props

Imported by Microsoft.NET.Sdk.props when the project extension is .vbproj. Defaults for WarningLevel, NoWarn, OptionExplicit, OptionCompare, OptionStrict, OptionInfer, WarningsAsErrors (adds NU1605) and DefineDebug / DefineTrace per configuration.

Sdks/Microsoft.NET.Sdk/targets/Microsoft.NET.Sdk.VisualBasic.targets

Imported by Microsoft.NET.Sdk.targets when the language is VB. The implicit Import items, FinalDefineConstants, the VBRuntime / UseReferencedVBRuntime logic, DisableSdkPath, the _MyType="Empty" define, the SupportsHotReload capability and the SYSLIB0011 rule.

Roslyn/Microsoft.VisualBasic.Core.targets

The CoreCompile target, which calls the Vbc task with 90 parameters, each fed by one property or item (listed below).

Roslyn/Microsoft.Managed.Core.targets

Behaviour shared with C#: UseSharedCompilation (default true), analyzer skipping, the Features property, source link and embedded files.

Because those are plain text files in the installed SDK, every statement about defaults on this page can be checked on your machine with dotnet msbuild -getProperty:Name, and the files are the authoritative reference when the documentation lags behind (it does, as the sections below point out).

The default items and the NETSDK1022 error

The glob is the single most common cause of a first migration error: a project converted from the old format still lists every file, so the SDK sees each file twice.

<!-- P.vbproj : SDK-style project that also lists a file the glob already included -->
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <RootNamespace>P</RootNamespace>
    <NuGetAudit>false</NuGetAudit>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <Compile Include="Program.vb" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>
$ dotnet build
/usr/share/dotnet/sdk/10.0.402/Sdks/Microsoft.NET.Sdk/targets/Microsoft.NET.Sdk.DefaultItems.Shared.targets(190,5): error NETSDK1022: Duplicate 'Compile' items were included. The .NET SDK includes 'Compile' items from your project directory by default. You can

(The message continues with the two ways out; the line is cut here.) You either delete the Compile item, or switch the glob off with EnableDefaultCompileItems set to false and list every file yourself. To exclude files from the glob, use Remove:

  <ItemGroup>
    <Compile Remove="Old/**" />
  </ItemGroup>

With Old/Legacy.vb (a second Sub Main in the same folder tree) the project built with 0 warnings and 0 errors and printed main, and dotnet msbuild -getItem:Compile listed only Program.vb: the removed file was never compiled. With EnableDefaultCompileItems set to false and <Compile Include="Program.vb" /> the same query also listed only Program.vb. Built and run: 2 projects.

Source: .NET project SDKs, MSBuild items, Customize your build

From project properties to vbc options

dotnet build does not understand Visual Basic; it asks MSBuild to evaluate the project and run its targets. One of those targets, CoreCompile, calls the Vbc task, and the task turns property values into a command line for the Roslyn Visual Basic compiler. So a property is never "applied" by the compiler: each property named below is read by the SDK’s targets and turned into zero or more vbc options. The diagram shows the path, and the table after it lists the option each property produces.

flowchart TD subgraph Evaluate["1. Evaluation: properties and items"] A["Directory.Build.props, then the .vbproj body, then -p:Name=Value from the command line"] B["Microsoft.NET.Sdk.VisualBasic.props sets OptionStrict Off, OptionExplicit On, OptionInfer On, OptionCompare Binary, NoWarn, DefineDebug, DefineTrace"] C["Microsoft.NET.Sdk.VisualBasic.targets builds Import items, FinalDefineConstants, VBRuntime, DisableSdkPath"] D["Items: Compile, Reference, Import, EmbeddedResource, Analyzer, AdditionalFiles, LinkResource"] A --> B --> C end subgraph Compile["2. CoreCompile target"] E["Vbc task in Microsoft.VisualBasic.Core.targets: 90 parameters, each fed by one property or item"] F["Command line written to a response file, one option per line"] G{"UseSharedCompilation"} H["VBCSCompiler build server, reused between builds"] I["vbc.dll in a new process"] E --> F --> G G -->|true, the default| H G -->|false| I end C --> E D --> E H --> J["obj/Debug/net10.0: App.dll, App.pdb, App.xml, refint/App.dll"] I --> J

The second diagram groups the properties by what they control and shows the vbc options they become. Where a property has no option of its own (Configuration, DefineDebug) it feeds an option indirectly; the full table is in the property reference and the option side is in the vbc option reference.

flowchart LR subgraph Props["MSBuild properties and items"] P1["OutputType, AssemblyName, RootNamespace, StartupObject, PlatformTarget"] P2["LangVersion, OptionStrict, OptionExplicit, OptionInfer, OptionCompare, RemoveIntegerChecks"] P3["DefineConstants, DefineDebug, DefineTrace, Configuration, TargetFramework"] P4["Import items, DisableImplicitNamespaceImports, MyType, VBRuntime"] P5["NoWarn, WarningLevel, TreatWarningsAsErrors, WarningsAsErrors, WarningsNotAsErrors"] P6["Optimize, DebugType, DebugSymbols, Deterministic, PathMap, ProduceReferenceAssembly"] P7["GenerateDocumentationFile, DocumentationFile, ErrorLog, CodeAnalysisRuleSet"] P8["Reference, ProjectReference, PackageReference, Analyzer, EmbeddedResource items"] end subgraph Opts["vbc options"] O1["-target, -out, -rootnamespace, -main, -platform"] O2["-langversion, -optionstrict, -optionexplicit, -optioninfer, -optioncompare, -removeintchecks"] O3["-define"] O4["-imports, -vbruntime, -nosdkpath"] O5["-nowarn, -warnaserror"] O6["-optimize, -debug, -deterministic, -pathmap, -refout"] O7["-doc, -errorlog, -ruleset"] O8["-reference, -analyzer, -resource"] end P1 --> O1 P2 --> O2 P3 --> O3 P4 --> O4 P5 --> O5 P6 --> O6 P7 --> O7 P8 --> O8

The real command line

The next project sets 18 properties and one Import item. It is a deliberately busy .vbproj; every property is explained in the sections below.

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <RootNamespace>Ks</RootNamespace>
    <AssemblyName>Ks</AssemblyName>
    <StartupObject>Ks.Program</StartupObject>
    <LangVersion>latest</LangVersion>
    <OptionStrict>On</OptionStrict>
    <OptionExplicit>On</OptionExplicit>
    <OptionInfer>On</OptionInfer>
    <OptionCompare>Text</OptionCompare>
    <RemoveIntegerChecks>true</RemoveIntegerChecks>
    <DefineConstants>$(DefineConstants),FEATURE_X=1,GREETING="hi"</DefineConstants>
    <GenerateDocumentationFile>true</GenerateDocumentationFile>
    <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
    <WarningsNotAsErrors>BC42024</WarningsNotAsErrors>
    <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);BC42350</NoWarn>
    <Deterministic>true</Deterministic>
    <DebugType>embedded</DebugType>
    <Optimize>false</Optimize>
    <PlatformTarget>x64</PlatformTarget>
    <NuGetAudit>false</NuGetAudit>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <Import Include="System.Text" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>

dotnet build -v:diag prints the command line the Vbc task ran. Shown here one option per line with the 167 reference assemblies and a few paths shortened and the NETnn_0_OR_GREATER version symbols dropped from /define:

<sdk>/Roslyn/bincore/vbc
/noconfig
/imports:System.Text,Microsoft.VisualBasic,System,System.Collections,System.Collections.Generic,System.Diagnostics,System.Linq,System.Xml.Linq,System.Threading.Tasks
/optioncompare:Text
/optionexplicit+
/optionstrict+
/nowarn:41999,42016,42017,42018,42019,42020,42021,42022,42032,42036,BC42350,BC41997
/nosdkpath
/optioninfer+
/nostdlib
/errorreport:prompt
/platform:x64
/removeintchecks+
/rootnamespace:Ks
/highentropyva+

(<sdk> is /usr/share/dotnet/sdk/10.0.402 and <ref> is the .NET 10 reference pack folder.) Read it against the project:

  • OptionCompare Text became /optioncompare:Text; OptionStrict On became /optionstrict+; RemoveIntegerChecks became /removeintchecks+.

  • NoWarn got the SDK’s default list plus BC42350 plus BC41997, which the SDK appends for .NET (Core) targets. The leading BC is accepted.

  • DefineConstants is a comma separated list; the SDK prepends CONFIG, DEBUG, TRACE and PLATFORM, leaves an empty entry (,,) where the empty $(DefineConstants) was, and appends _MyType="Empty" and the framework symbols. The string value GREETING="hi" had its quotes escaped.

  • StartupObject became /main:Ks.Program, and GenerateDocumentationFile became /doc: with a path under obj.

  • TreatWarningsAsErrors became /warnaserror+, WarningsNotAsErrors a trailing /warnaserror-:BC42024, and the SDK’s own WarningsAsErrors (NU1605;SYSLIB0011) a /warnaserror+: list.

  • /noconfig, /nostdlib, /nosdkpath, /errorreport:prompt, /highentropyva+, /filealign:512, /utf8output, /refout: and the two analyzers were not asked for: they are SDK defaults.

  • The generated AssemblyInfo.vb and the assembly-attributes file are compiled together with your source.

The command line is the same one you would type by hand (see Running vbc by hand); only -v:diag or a binary log shows it during a normal build.

Printing the command line without compiling

Reading -v:diag output (it is roughly 50,000 lines for a tiny project) is clumsy. The SDK has a switch meant for IDEs, ProvideCommandLineArgs, which makes the Vbc task return its arguments as an item instead of running the compiler. With the -getTargetResult switch of dotnet msbuild you get one JSON entry per argument:

dotnet msbuild Map.vbproj -nologo -v:q -t:ResolveReferences,CoreCompile \
  -p:SkipCompilerExecution=true -p:ProvideCommandLineArgs=true -getTargetResult:CoreCompile

This is how every row of the property table below was produced: the command is run with the baseline project and once more with one extra -p:Name=Value, and the lines that changed are the option(s) that property controls. The baseline (a dotnet new console -lang VB project renamed Map, default configuration) is:

The first surprise is /optionstrict:custom. The SDK’s default of OptionStrict Off does not become /optionstrict-; it becomes custom, a mode that raises the individual Option Strict diagnostics as warnings. Those warnings (BC42016 to BC42022 and a few more) are then silenced by the SDK’s default NoWarn, which is why a default project accepts implicit narrowing silently. The consequence is demonstrated in The NoWarn trap.

The Configuration changes the generated options as follows (captured with the same method, one extra -p:Configuration=...):

Configuration Symbols in /define Debug options Other options

Debug (default)

CONFIG="Debug", DEBUG=-1, TRACE=-1

/debug+ and /debug:portable

/optimize-, output under obj/Debug/net10.0

Release

CONFIG="Release", TRACE=-1, RELEASE=-1

/debug-

/optimize+, output under obj/Release/net10.0

Staging (a custom name)

CONFIG="Staging", STAGING=-1 (no TRACE, no DEBUG)

/debug-

/optimize-, output under obj/Staging/net10.0

The symbol that equals the upper-cased configuration name (RELEASE, STAGING) comes from ImplicitConfigurationDefine; set DisableImplicitConfigurationDefines to true to stop that. DEBUG and TRACE come from DefineDebug and DefineTrace, which the VB .props file sets per configuration. Setting DefineDebug to false on a Debug configuration does not remove DEBUG: the observed list still contains DEBUG=-1 (it moves to the end), because the implicit configuration define re-adds it. To really drop DEBUG in a Debug build, change Configuration, or set DisableImplicitConfigurationDefines and DefineDebug to false together.

Properties that do nothing in Visual Basic

C# project files and templates use several properties that look portable and are not. For each, the table says what was tested.

Property or item Result in a VB project

Nullable

No effect. Nullable enable produced no change in the vbc command line. Visual Basic has no nullable reference types; String is always nullable.

ImplicitUsings, <Using Include="...">

No effect. With ImplicitUsings enable and <Using Include="System.Text" />, Dim sb As New StringBuilder() failed with error BC30002: Type 'StringBuilder' is not defined.; replacing the Using item with <Import Include="System.Text" /> compiled and ran. The VB mstest template still writes both, harmlessly.

LangVersion preview

Rejected by the build: vbc : error BC2014: the value 'preview' is invalid for option 'langversion'. VB has no preview versions.

AllowUnsafeBlocks, CheckForOverflowUnderflow

No effect: neither changed the vbc command line. VB has no unsafe code; the nearest equivalent of the second is RemoveIntegerChecks (inverted meaning).

InvariantGlobalization

Not a compiler setting: it is written to runtimeconfig.json and read by the .NET runtime, so it works the same in VB.

What the properties do at run time

The next project reads its own build settings back, so one program shows five properties at once: RootNamespace, Version, OptionCompare, RemoveIntegerChecks and the conditional-compilation symbols. The project file sets OptionStrict and TreatWarningsAsErrors, and DefineConstants with two symbols of its own. Its root namespace is Shelf.Build. The code has no Imports for System, System.Collections.Generic or System.Linq: they come from the SDK’s implicit Import items.

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <RootNamespace>Shelf.Build</RootNamespace>
    <OptionStrict>On</OptionStrict>
    <Version>1.2.3-beta.1</Version>
    <DefineConstants>$(DefineConstants),FEATURE_LOANS=True,EDITION="Community"</DefineConstants>
    <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
    <NuGetAudit>false</NuGetAudit>
  </PropertyGroup>

</Project>
Option Strict On

Imports System.Reflection

Namespace Reports

    Public Module Program

        Public Sub Main()
            ' No Imports statement names System, System.Collections.Generic or System.Linq:
            ' they come from the SDK's implicit Import items.
            Dim titles As New List(Of String) From {"Dune", "Emma"}
            Console.WriteLine("Titles: " & String.Join(", ", titles.OrderBy(Function(t) t)))

            Console.WriteLine("Type name: " & GetType(Program).FullName)
            Console.WriteLine("Assembly:  " & Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly().GetName().Name)

            Dim info As String = Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly() _
                .GetCustomAttribute(Of AssemblyInformationalVersionAttribute)().InformationalVersion
            Console.WriteLine("Version:   " & info.Split("+"c)(0))

            Console.WriteLine("Option Compare: ""a"" = ""A"" is " & ("a" = "A").ToString())

            Dim big As Integer = Integer.MaxValue
            Try
                big += 1
                Console.WriteLine("Integer overflow check: removed (wrapped to " & big.ToString() & ")")
            Catch ex As OverflowException
                Console.WriteLine("Integer overflow check: active (" & ex.GetType().Name & ")")
            End Try

            Dim symbols As New List(Of String)
#If DEBUG Then
            symbols.Add("DEBUG")
#End If
#If TRACE Then
            symbols.Add("TRACE")
#End If
#If NET10_0_OR_GREATER Then
            symbols.Add("NET10_0_OR_GREATER")
#End If
#If FEATURE_LOANS Then
            symbols.Add("FEATURE_LOANS")
#End If
#If CONFIG = "Release" Then
            symbols.Add("CONFIG=Release")
#ElseIf CONFIG = "Debug" Then
            symbols.Add("CONFIG=Debug")
#End If
#If EDITION = "Community" Then
            symbols.Add("EDITION=Community")
#End If
            Console.WriteLine("Symbols:   " & String.Join(" ", symbols))
        End Sub

    End Module

End Namespace

Five builds of the same source, each with --no-incremental into its own output folder (dotnet build -o out/<label>), then dotnet out/<label>/Props.dll. Each run changes one thing on the command line. A command-line -p: property wins over the project file:

== debug: dotnet build
Titles: Dune, Emma

Read the outputs against the properties. Namespace Reports in the code became Shelf.Build.Reports, and Acme.Reports when the root namespace changed: the Namespace statement never contains the root namespace. The assembly name is Props, from the file name, whatever the root namespace says. The informational version is the Version value with the + and commit hash that the SDK appends when source control information is present; the code strips that suffix before printing. Release removed DEBUG and TRACE stayed. RemoveIntegerChecks turned Integer.MaxValue + 1 from an OverflowException into a silent wrap to -2147483648: a program whose output depends on a project property needs the property in its documentation. OptionCompare Text made "a" = "A" true for the whole project, which a file-level Option Compare Binary would override again. Built and run: 1 project, 5 builds.

Source: -removeintchecks, -rootnamespace, -optioncompare

Project settings that break or change the build

Each of the following projects is the default Exe project for net10.0 with root namespace E plus the one line shown. The lines printed are the diagnostics of dotnet build (the Build succeeded summary is omitted). Several are errors that only appear because a project property was set; they are the messages you will meet when you change a setting in an existing solution.

OptionStrict in the project file

<OptionStrict>On</OptionStrict>
Public Module Program
    Public Sub Main()
        Dim price As Decimal = 12.5D
        Dim whole As Integer = price
        Dim anything As Object = whole
        Console.WriteLine(anything.Length)
    End Sub
End Module
Program.vb(4,32): error BC30512: Option Strict On disallows implicit conversions from 'Decimal' to 'Integer'.
Program.vb(6,27): error BC30574: Option Strict On disallows late binding.

The same two statements build with 0 warnings and 0 errors under the SDK default (OptionStrict Off, which vbc receives as /optionstrict:custom), and the late-bound anything.Length is only found at run time: run in that default project, the narrowing silently rounded 3.5 to 4 and the late-bound Length call on an Integer threw MissingMemberException. This is the whole case for setting OptionStrict in Directory.Build.props, as the Shelf solution does. The error list of Option Strict On is on Option Statements.

OptionExplicit

Public Module Program
    Public Sub Main()
        total = 3
        Console.WriteLine(total)
    End Sub
End Module
Program.vb(3,9): error BC30451: 'total' is not declared. It may be inaccessible due to its protection level.
Program.vb(4,27): error BC30451: 'total' is not declared. It may be inaccessible due to its protection level.

With <OptionExplicit>Off</OptionExplicit> the same file builds with 0 warnings and 0 errors, and total becomes an implicitly declared Object. Nothing in a modern project has a reason to switch it off. A file can still say Option Explicit Off, which wins over the project.

Implicit imports switched off

DisableImplicitNamespaceImports set to true removes the SDK’s eight Import items (all of Microsoft.VisualBasic, System, System.Collections, System.Collections.Generic, System.Diagnostics, System.Linq, System.Xml.Linq, System.Threading.Tasks):

Public Module Program
    Public Sub Main()
        Dim names As New List(Of String)
        Console.WriteLine(names.Count)
    End Sub
End Module
Program.vb(3,26): error BC30002: Type 'List' is not defined.
Program.vb(4,9): error BC30451: 'Console' is not declared. It may be inaccessible due to its protection level.

Every file now needs its own Imports System and Imports System.Collections.Generic. This is the setting to use when you want a project where nothing is imported without being written; the price is that Microsoft.VisualBasic is no longer imported either: Left("abc", 2) then fails with error BC30451: 'Left' is not declared. It may be inaccessible due to its protection level. until the file says Imports Microsoft.VisualBasic. Keywords such as CInt are part of the language and keep working.

LangVersion

<LangVersion>14</LangVersion>
Public Module Program
    Public Sub Main()
        Dim pair = (Title:="Dune", Year:=1965)
        Dim big As Integer = 1_000_000
        Console.WriteLine(pair.Title & " " & big.ToString())
    End Sub
End Module
Program.vb(3,20): error BC36716: Visual Basic 14.0 does not support tuples.
Program.vb(4,30): error BC36716: Visual Basic 14.0 does not support digit separators.

With <LangVersion>15</LangVersion> the same file built with 0 warnings and 0 errors. With a value that does not exist (17.14) the compiler stops before reading any source: vbc : error BC2014: the value '17.14' is invalid for option 'langversion'.

Two entry points and StartupObject

Public Module First
    Public Sub Main()
        Console.WriteLine("First")
    End Sub
End Module

Public Module Second
    Public Sub Main()
        Console.WriteLine("Second")
    End Sub
End Module
vbc : error BC30738: 'Sub Main' is declared more than once in 'E': E.First.Main(), E.Second.Main()

With <StartupObject>E.Second</StartupObject> (the root namespace E plus the module name; without the root namespace prefix the name is not found) the program built and printed Second.

Warnings policy

One file with an unused local variable:

Option Strict On

Public Module Program
    Public Sub Main()
        Dim unused As Integer
        Console.WriteLine("hello")
    End Sub
End Module
Project line(s) Result

(none)

Program.vb(5,13): warning BC42024: Unused local variable: 'unused'.

<TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>

Program.vb(5,13): error BC42024: Unused local variable: 'unused'.

TreatWarningsAsErrors true and <WarningsNotAsErrors>BC42024</WarningsNotAsErrors>

Program.vb(5,13): warning BC42024: ... (still a warning; build succeeds)

<WarningsAsErrors>$(WarningsAsErrors);BC42024</WarningsAsErrors>

Program.vb(5,13): error BC42024: ...

<NoWarn>$(NoWarn);BC42024</NoWarn> and TreatWarningsAsErrors true

nothing: the warning is suppressed before it can be escalated

The NoWarn trap

The SDK’s default NoWarn hides BC42016 to BC42022, the warnings of the custom Option Strict mode. Assigning NoWarn without $(NoWarn) throws that list away and makes those warnings appear in every file of the project:

Public Module Program
    Public Sub Main()
        Dim count As Integer = 3.5
        Console.WriteLine(count)
    End Sub
End Module
<NoWarn>BC42024</NoWarn>
Program.vb(3,32): warning BC42016: Implicit conversion from 'Double' to 'Integer'.

With the default NoWarn the same file builds silently (and prints 4: the narrowing is real, only the warning is hidden). Write <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);BC42024</NoWarn> to append. A project that sets OptionStrict to On is not exposed to this trap, because there is nothing left to warn about.

OptionStrict is a Boolean in MSBuild

The Vbc task declares OptionStrict as a Boolean, so the third state of the language statement (Option Strict Custom does not exist as a statement either) is not available as a project value:

<OptionStrict>Custom</OptionStrict>
Microsoft.VisualBasic.Core.targets(103,10): error MSB4030: "Custom" is an invalid value for the "OptionStrict" parameter of the "Vbc" task. The "OptionStrict" parameter is of type "System.Boolean".

Off is what already gives the custom mode, as the command lines above show.

DefineConstants separators

DefineConstants is passed to /define, which separates entries by commas. The semicolon that MSBuild uses elsewhere (and that C# projects use for this very property) breaks the build:

<DefineConstants>ALPHA=1;BETA=True</DefineConstants>
vbc : error BC31030: Conditional compilation constant 'ALPHA=1 ^^ ^^ ;BETA=True' is not valid: End of statement expected.

Appending with $(DefineConstants);ALPHA=1;BETA=True fails the same way (BC31030, "Identifier expected" for the empty first entry). Both of

<DefineConstants>ALPHA=1,BETA=True</DefineConstants>
<DefineConstants>$(DefineConstants),ALPHA=1,BETA=True</DefineConstants>

built, and a program using #If ALPHA = 1, #If BETA and #If DEBUG printed ALPHA is 1, BETA is on, DEBUG is on. The ordering of the options the task writes (a ,, empty entry for an empty $(DefineConstants)) is harmless. Built and run: 19 small projects in this section, plus 4 variants of the DefineConstants project.

Source: -define, -nowarn, -warnaserror, -main

LangVersion

LangVersion limits the compiler to the syntax of an older Visual Basic version and nothing else: it does not change the target framework, the library surface or the runtime behaviour. It becomes /langversion:<value>. The compiler itself lists what it accepts:

$ vbc -langversion:?
Supported language versions:
default
9
10
11
12
14
15
15.3
15.5
16
16.9
17.13 (default)
latest

Note that the list ends at 17.13 and has no 17 or 17.0. Each candidate value was passed to the real compiler:

7, 8, 13

error BC2014: the value '7' is invalid for option 'langversion' (the same text for the others)

9, 9.0

accepted (9 is the oldest language version this compiler accepts)

10, 11, 12, 14, 14.0, 15, 15.0, 15.3, 15.5, 16, 16.0, 16.9, 17.13

accepted (a whole number may be written with .0)

default, latest, Latest

accepted; both mean 17.13 on this SDK; the value is not case sensitive

17, 17.0, 17.9, 17.14, 18, preview

error BC2014: the value '17.14' is invalid for option 'langversion' (the same text for the others)

default means the latest major version and latest the latest version including minor versions; they are the same today because the last one is a minor version of 17. The compiler -help text says the same. VB 17.0 added consumption of CallerArgumentExpression and 17.13 honours OverloadResolutionPriority and the unmanaged constraint, but neither is a syntax change, which is why neither has a LangVersion value of its own other than the final 17.13.

The gates match the history of the language and the Learn what’s-new page: auto-implemented properties arrived with 10, Async and iterators with 11, interpolation and ?. with 14, tuples and digit separators with 15, non-trailing named arguments and Private Protected with 15.5 (the compiler says BC30241 for the first before 15.5). A library that must compile for an old consumer’s language version can therefore pin LangVersion and get an error on any newer syntax. Nothing in the language added syntax after 15.5 apart from places where a comment is now allowed (16.0); the later versions (16.9, 17.0, 17.13) are consumption features: init-only properties, required members, OverloadResolutionPriority and CallerArgumentExpression need no new syntax. See History, Versions and Language Strategy for the story.

Where the documentation lags: the Learn -langversion page and the "Select the Visual Basic language version" page list values only up to 16.9, and the -langversion page says the option can be set "only by using the command line" (its sibling page describes the project property and Directory.Build.props, which is the one that is right: <LangVersion> in the project file produces the option, as the 14 example above showed, and the compiler accepts 17.13). Built and run: 10 probes by 11 versions, plus the value list.

Source: -langversion, Select the Visual Basic language version, What’s new for Visual Basic

Global imports and the missing global using

C# 10 introduced global using and ImplicitUsings. Visual Basic had global imports first, and they are an item of the project, not a statement of the language: <Import Include="System.Text" /> becomes an entry in /imports:. There is no Global Imports statement; each file still declares its own Imports. The SDK adds eight Import items for you (the eight namespaces in the table above; System.Data is the ninth when the target is .NET Framework). The VB templates add more:

Template Import items written into the .vbproj

console, classlib, mstest, xunit, nunit

none (the SDK ones apply)

winforms

System.Data, System.Drawing, System.Windows.Forms

wpf

System.Windows, System.Windows.Controls, System.Windows.Data, System.Windows.Documents, System.Windows.Input, System.Windows.Media, System.Windows.Media.Imaging, System.Windows.Navigation, System.Windows.Shapes

The Import item in a project must not be confused with MSBuild’s own <Import Project="..." /> element, which pulls in another project file. They look alike and are unrelated. Two further behaviours follow from the tests above:

  • Setting UseWindowsForms or UseWPF does not add Import items; the template does. If you create the project by hand, add them yourself.

  • The VB mstest template still writes a C#-style <Using Include="..." /> item that does nothing in VB (see the table of properties that do nothing). The tests use an ordinary Imports statement in the file.

An alias is possible in a file (Imports Sb = System.Text.StringBuilder) but not as a project-wide import. Because the compiler imports nothing implicitly beyond this list, a type of another namespace (StringBuilder, Regex, HttpClient) always needs a file-level Imports or an Import item, exactly as in the failing ImplicitUsings example above.

(the code is #If VBC_VER >= 17.13 Then, #If _MyType = "Empty" Then, #If PLATFORM = "AnyCPU" Then, #If NET10_0 Then, #If NETFRAMEWORK Then with #Else.) Comparing a string symbol with a string literal works in #If. The #If directive, #Const and the Conditional attribute are on Conditional Compilation and Directives. The three gotchas of the property itself:

  • The separator is a comma (shown above); a semicolon fails with BC31030.

  • A string symbol is written with plain double quotes in the element (EDITION="Community", as in the demonstration above); the generated command line escapes them.

  • DefineDebug false does not remove DEBUG (see the Configuration table).

MyType and the Visual Basic runtime

Two groups of settings decide what the Microsoft.VisualBasic library looks like to the program. MyType selects the My classes the compiler generates; VBRuntime selects which Microsoft.VisualBasic is linked. The SDK’s own comment in Microsoft.NET.Sdk.VisualBasic.targets states the defaults, and the captured command lines agree with it:

Target /vbruntime option observed Why

net10.0, net8.0

/vbruntime:<reference pack>/Microsoft.VisualBasic.dll

UseReferencedVBRuntime is true for .NET Core 3.0 and later: the runtime is the Microsoft.VisualBasic among the references.

net10.0-windows with UseWindowsForms

/vbruntime:.../microsoft.windowsdesktop.app.ref/10.0.13/ref/net10.0/Microsoft.VisualBasic.dll

The Windows Desktop reference pack contains the runtime with the Windows Forms application services.

net481

/vbruntime:.../microsoft.netframework.referenceassemblies.net481/1.0.3/build/.NETFramework/v4.8.1/Microsoft.VisualBasic.dll

The .NET Framework’s own Microsoft.VisualBasic.dll, found in the reference assemblies package that the SDK downloads, which is why net481 builds even on Linux.

netstandard2.0

/vbruntime*

VBRuntime Embed: the runtime is compiled into your assembly, because no Microsoft.VisualBasic.dll is available for netstandard.

For a library that targets netstandard2.0 the embedded runtime means the library carries its own copy of the Visual Basic runtime functions it uses, and some runtime functions are not available to it (the effects are on Libraries, Packaging and Deployment). The properties are VBRuntime (a path, Embed or Default), UseReferencedVBRuntime and NoVBRuntimeReference; MyType is a plain string whose values include Console, Windows, WindowsForms, WindowsFormsWithCustomSubMain, Web, Empty and Custom. On .NET 10, Console fails with BC30002 ("Type …​ is not defined") and Web does not build at all; Empty is the default and the right choice for console programs and libraries. WindowsFormsWithCustomSubMain is for Windows Forms projects that write their own Sub Main, as the template does. The My namespace and what each value generates are on The My Namespace.

A complete example is a library Lib that targets net10.0;net481, with Platform.Describe returning a different string per target through the symbols, and a net10.0 console program that references it. The project of the library:

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFrameworks>net10.0;net481</TargetFrameworks>
    <RootNamespace>Shelf.Lib</RootNamespace>
    <OptionStrict>On</OptionStrict>
    <NuGetAudit>false</NuGetAudit>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup Condition="'$(TargetFramework)' == 'net481'">
    <Reference Include="System.Net.Http" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>
Option Strict On

Public NotInheritable Class Platform

    Private Sub New()
    End Sub

    Public Shared Function Describe() As String
#If NETFRAMEWORK Then
        Return ".NET Framework build (NET481 defined)"
#ElseIf NET10_0_OR_GREATER Then
        Return ".NET 10 build (NET10_0_OR_GREATER defined)"
#Else
        Return "other build"
#End If
    End Function

End Class
$ dotnet build App
  Lib -> Lib/bin/Debug/net10.0/Lib.dll
  App -> App/bin/Debug/net10.0/App.dll
$ dotnet run --project App --no-build
.NET 10 build (NET10_0_OR_GREATER defined)
$ dotnet build Lib -f net481
  Lib -> Lib/bin/Debug/net481/Lib.dll

A consumer that targets net10.0 makes MSBuild build only the matching target of the library, so bin/Debug held only net10.0 after the first build. dotnet build Lib -f net481 built the other one, on Linux, using the reference assemblies package. A net481 build can be compiled anywhere but run only on Windows. The conditional Reference item is the usual way to add an assembly that only the .NET Framework target needs. Built and run: 3 projects (the net481 output compiled, not run).

Source: Target frameworks, Cross-platform targeting

Sharing settings across a solution

Every setting above belongs in the project file if it is specific to the project and in one of four solution-level files if it is shared. MSBuild looks upward from each project directory, and the first file of each kind it finds is imported automatically: Directory.Build.props before the project body (so project files can override it), Directory.Build.targets after the SDK targets (so it can override them), Directory.Packages.props for central package versions, and global.json (read by the dotnet host) for the SDK version. The buildprops, buildtargets, packagesprops, globaljson, editorconfig, nugetconfig and gitignore short names of dotnet new create starters for them.

The experiment: a repository with Directory.Build.props (sets TargetFramework, OptionStrict On, LangVersion, TreatWarningsAsErrors, Deterministic, Version and ManagePackageVersionsCentrally), Directory.Build.targets (prints the effective values after every build), Directory.Packages.props (one PackageVersion) and global.json; and two projects, src/Core that adds nothing and src/Tools that sets OptionStrict Off and Version 0.1.0.

<!-- Directory.Build.props -->
<Project>

  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <OptionStrict>On</OptionStrict>
    <LangVersion>latest</LangVersion>
    <TreatWarningsAsErrors>true</TreatWarningsAsErrors>
    <Deterministic>true</Deterministic>
    <Version>2.0.0</Version>
    <NuGetAudit>false</NuGetAudit>
    <ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>true</ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>
  </PropertyGroup>

</Project>

<!-- Directory.Build.targets -->
<Project>

  <Target Name="ShowOptions" AfterTargets="Build">
    <Message Importance="high" Text="$(MSBuildProjectName): OptionStrict=$(OptionStrict) Version=$(Version) RootNamespace=$(RootNamespace)" />
  </Target>

</Project>

<!-- Directory.Packages.props -->
<Project>

  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions" Version="10.0.0" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>

<!-- global.json -->
{ "sdk": { "version": "10.0.100", "rollForward": "latestFeature" } }

<!-- src/Core/Core.vbproj -->
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <RootNamespace>Shelf.Core</RootNamespace>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>

<!-- src/Tools/Tools.vbproj -->
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <RootNamespace>Shelf.Tools</RootNamespace>
    <OptionStrict>Off</OptionStrict>
    <Version>0.1.0</Version>
  </PropertyGroup>

</Project>

(The PackageReference in Core.vbproj has no Version: with central package management the version comes from Directory.Packages.props.)

$ dotnet build src/Core
  Core: OptionStrict=On Version=2.0.0 RootNamespace=Shelf.Core
$ dotnet build src/Tools
  Tools: OptionStrict=Off Version=0.1.0 RootNamespace=Shelf.Tools
$ dotnet msbuild src/Core/Core.vbproj -getProperty:OptionStrict,TreatWarningsAsErrors,Version
OptionStrict: On   TreatWarningsAsErrors: true   Version: 2.0.0
$ dotnet msbuild src/Tools/Tools.vbproj -getProperty:OptionStrict,TreatWarningsAsErrors,Version
OptionStrict: Off  TreatWarningsAsErrors: true   Version: 0.1.0
$ dotnet msbuild src/Tools/Tools.vbproj -p:OptionStrict=On -getProperty:OptionStrict
On
$ dotnet --version
10.0.402
$ dotnet list src/Core package
   Top-level Package                                Requested   Resolved
   > Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions      10.0.0      10.0.0

(-getProperty prints JSON; the two JSON objects are shown as one line each.) The project value won over Directory.Build.props (Tools kept Off and 0.1.0); the command-line -p:OptionStrict=On won over the project; global.json asked for 10.0.100 with latestFeature and the installed 10.0.402 satisfied it. The central package version 10.0.0 was applied to a PackageReference without a Version. Built and run: 2 projects.

Nested files. Only the nearest Directory.Build.props is imported. A file deeper in the tree that wants the parent’s settings imports it explicitly, which is what a tests folder normally does. This was run with tests/Directory.Build.props:

<Project>

  <Import Project="$([MSBuild]::GetPathOfFileAbove('Directory.Build.props', '$(MSBuildThisFileDirectory)../'))" />

  <PropertyGroup>
    <IsPackable>false</IsPackable>
    <WarningsNotAsErrors>$(WarningsNotAsErrors);BC42024</WarningsNotAsErrors>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <Import Include="System.Text" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>

The test project got the parent’s OptionStrict On, TreatWarningsAsErrors true and Company Shelf, plus IsPackable false, WarningsNotAsErrors ;BC42024 and a ninth Import item System.Text; the project in src/ got only the parent’s values and IsPackable true. Built and run: 2 projects.

The Shelf reference solution of this site sets OptionStrict, TreatWarningsAsErrors and NuGetAudit in one Directory.Build.props, which is what you should do for any multi-project Visual Basic repository: it makes OptionStrict On a solution policy instead of a per-file chore. The .editorconfig keys for style and analyzer severity are on XML Documentation, Analyzers and Code Style.

Source: Customize your build, Central Package Management, global.json overview

The dotnet command line for Visual Basic

Everything in an IDE is available from the dotnet command, and the command is what continuous integration runs (see Testing for CI). The default language of dotnet new is C#; a Visual Basic project needs -lang VB (or --language VB). The templates that have a Visual Basic version on SDK 10.0.402 (dotnet new list --language VB):

Template Name                  Short Name           Language  Tags
-----------------------------  -------------------  --------  -----------------------
Class Library                  classlib             C#,F#,VB  Common/Library
Console App                    console              C#,F#,VB  Common/Console
MSTest Test Class              mstest-class         C#,F#,VB  Test/MSTest
MSTest Test Project            mstest               C#,F#,VB  Test/MSTest/Desktop/Web
NUnit Test Item                nunit-test           C#,F#,VB  Test/NUnit
NUnit Test Project             nunit                C#,F#,VB  Test/NUnit/Desktop/Web
Windows Forms App              winforms             C#,VB     Common/WinForms
Windows Forms Class Library    winformslib          C#,VB     Common/WinForms
Windows Forms Control Library  winformscontrollib   C#,VB     Common/WinForms
WPF Application                wpf                  C#,VB     Common/WPF
WPF Class Library              wpflib               C#,VB     Common/WPF
WPF Custom Control Library     wpfcustomcontrollib  C#,VB     Common/WPF
WPF User Control Library       wpfusercontrollib    C#,VB     Common/WPF
xUnit Test Project             xunit                C#,F#,VB  Test/xUnit/Desktop/Web

There is no Visual Basic webapi, web, blazor, worker, grpc or MAUI template; the list above is the complete VB set. The configuration-file templates (sln, slnf, globaljson, editorconfig, nugetconfig, gitignore, gitattributes, tool-manifest, buildprops, buildtargets, packagesprops, webconfig) have no language and apply to any project. The console template’s own options show how little VB-specific there is: -f/--framework (one choice, net10.0), --langVersion (writes LangVersion), --no-restore and --aot.

A complete workflow

The following session builds the Shelf skeleton used by the other pages: a library, a console program that uses it and an MSTest project. The commands are the real ones; the Directory.Build.props was written first (it sets OptionStrict On, TreatWarningsAsErrors true and NuGetAudit false, see above). First the scaffolding:

dotnet new sln -n Shelf
dotnet new classlib -lang VB -o Shelf.Core
dotnet new console -lang VB -o Shelf.Cli
dotnet new mstest -lang VB -o Shelf.Tests
dotnet sln add Shelf.Core Shelf.Cli Shelf.Tests
dotnet add Shelf.Cli reference Shelf.Core
dotnet add Shelf.Tests reference Shelf.Core
dotnet add Shelf.Core package Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions --version 10.0.0

dotnet list Shelf.Cli reference

(Some chatty lines of the restore were left out.) dotnet new sln wrote Shelf.slnx, the XML solution format that is the default in SDK 10; its whole content is three Project Path elements. Existing .sln files keep working and dotnet sln Old.sln migrate converted one: .slnx file /w/t/Old.slnx generated. Note that the dotnet add reference command put the ProjectReference in a new ItemGroup above the PropertyGroup, which is harmless: MSBuild does not care about the order of groups in the project body.

The dotnet new mstest project built and ran straight from the template under OptionStrict On and TreatWarningsAsErrors (Passed! - Failed: 0, Passed: 1, Skipped: 0, Total: 1), so the C#-style properties it carries are inert. Then the sources of the three projects were replaced:

Option Strict On

Namespace Domain

    Public NotInheritable Class Isbn

        Public ReadOnly Property Value As String

        Public Sub New(value As String)
            If Not IsValid(value) Then
                Throw New ArgumentException("Not a valid ISBN-13: " & value, NameOf(value))
            End If
            Me.Value = value
        End Sub

        Public Shared Function IsValid(value As String) As Boolean
            If value Is Nothing OrElse value.Length <> 13 Then
                Return False
            End If
            Dim sum As Integer = 0
            For i As Integer = 0 To 12
                If Not Char.IsDigit(value(i)) Then
                    Return False
                End If
                Dim digit As Integer = Asc(value(i)) - Asc("0"c)
                sum += If(i Mod 2 = 0, digit, digit * 3)
            Next
            Return sum Mod 10 = 0
        End Function

    End Class

End Namespace
Option Strict On

Imports Shelf.Core.Domain

Public Module Program

    Public Function Main(args As String()) As Integer
        Dim failures As Integer = 0
        For Each candidate As String In args
            If Isbn.IsValid(candidate) Then
                Console.WriteLine(candidate & " is a valid ISBN-13")
            Else
                Console.WriteLine(candidate & " is not valid")
                failures += 1
            End If
        Next
        Return failures
    End Function

End Module
Option Strict On

Imports Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting
Imports Shelf.Core.Domain

<TestClass>
Public Class IsbnTests

    <TestMethod>
    Public Sub Valid_isbn_is_accepted()
        Assert.IsTrue(Isbn.IsValid("9780306406157"))
    End Sub

    <TestMethod>
    Public Sub Wrong_check_digit_is_rejected()
        Assert.IsFalse(Isbn.IsValid("9780306406158"))
    End Sub

End Class

(The root namespaces are the project names, Shelf.Core, Shelf.Cli and Shelf.Tests, so Namespace Domain in the library is Shelf.Core.Domain; the console module and the test class sit in their project’s root namespace and need no Namespace block.) The commands that use them:

The ls pub listing is the second block of names: the apphost Shelf.Cli, its .deps.json and .runtimeconfig.json, the two assemblies and their PDBs. dotnet format --verify-no-changes and dotnet clean printed nothing of note for this solution.) -pp:expanded.xml produced a 1.5 MB file for the console project in which Directory.Build.props (line 94) comes long before the Visual Basic .props (line 1090) and the project body, which is why a project can override what the file sets. What each command does to the MSBuild model

Command MSBuild equivalent Visual Basic notes

dotnet restore

msbuild -t:Restore

Reads PackageReference, ProjectReference and Directory.Packages.props and writes obj/project.assets.json; build, run, test do it first unless --no-restore. Offline builds need the packages already in the NuGet cache.

dotnet build [-c Release] [-o dir] [-f tfm] [--no-restore] [--no-incremental] [-p:Name=Value] [-v:level] [-bl]

msbuild -t:Build

-p: sets a global property that beats the project file (shown above); -f selects one target of a multi-targeted project; -bl writes msbuild.binlog, readable with the MSBuild Structured Log Viewer, the best tool for "why did this property get that value" questions.

dotnet run [--project p] [-c cfg] [--no-build] [-- args]

build, then dotnet App.dll

Everything after -- goes to Main. The program’s return value is the exit code. A stale build after -p:StartupObject=... is a known trap: use dotnet build --no-incremental and then run.

dotnet test [project] [--filter ...]

build, then the test host

The VB mstest, xunit and nunit templates; see Testing for the runner differences. In this SDK the argument is a project path; a --solution switch is not accepted. --list-tests lists the test names without running them.

dotnet pack, dotnet publish

msbuild -t:Pack, -t:Publish

pack makes a .nupkg (a warning about the missing readme is normal); publish creates the deployable folder. Publish modes are on Libraries, Packaging and Deployment.

dotnet clean

msbuild -t:Clean

Deletes the outputs of the build.

dotnet sln add / remove / list / migrate

(solution file edit)

Works on .sln and .slnx; migrate writes the .slnx.

dotnet add reference / package, dotnet remove ..., dotnet list ...

(project file edit)

Edits the .vbproj; dotnet add package also restores (its output is the info : lines shown above).

dotnet format

(Roslyn workspace, not MSBuild targets)

Applies .editorconfig formatting and style rules; it supports Visual Basic.

dotnet msbuild

the same MSBuild engine

-getProperty:A,B, -getItem:Name and -getTargetResult:Target print values as JSON without building; -pp:out.xml writes the fully expanded project, with every imported file inlined in evaluation order, which is the best way to read the SDK’s contribution.

dotnet watch

(file watcher around run/test/build)

Hot Reload for VB: the VB targets add the SupportsHotReload capability for projects targeting .NET 6 or later (it is in Microsoft.NET.Sdk.VisualBasic.targets). Not run here; see Debugging and Diagnostics.

Two useful orientation commands: dotnet --list-sdks printed 10.0.402 [/usr/share/dotnet/sdk], and dotnet msbuild -getProperty:MSBuildVersion,NETCoreSdkVersion,VisualBasicTargetsPath,VisualBasicCoreTargetsPath printed 18.9.15, 10.0.402, /usr/share/dotnet/sdk/10.0.402/Microsoft.VisualBasic.CurrentVersion.targets and .../Sdks/Microsoft.NET.Sdk/targets/../../../Roslyn/Microsoft.VisualBasic.Core.targets: the last two are the files that do the work. Built and run: all of the above.

Source: dotnet new templates, dotnet build, dotnet run, dotnet test, dotnet pack, dotnet publish, dotnet sln, dotnet reference add, dotnet package add, dotnet format, dotnet msbuild

The vbc option reference

vbc is the Roslyn Visual Basic compiler. In the .NET SDK it is Roslyn/bincore/vbc.dll under the SDK folder (/usr/share/dotnet/sdk/10.0.402/Roslyn/bincore/vbc.dll in the container), a framework-dependent program started with dotnet; the vbc file next to it is its apphost. vbc -version printed 5.9.0-1.26505.111: that is the compiler version, not the language version (17.13, see above). Learn’s "compiler options listed by category" page and the individual option pages describe an older compiler; the table below is the output of vbc -help of this compiler, in its eight groups, plus five options the compiler accepts but does not list. The Learn page of an option (where one exists) is linked in the references. In the "Option" column [+|-] means the option may be followed by + (on), - (off) or nothing (on).

Each option below was passed to the SDK 10.0.402 compiler on a small module. All were accepted; the ones that take a file reported a problem with the (deliberately missing) file instead of "unrecognized option", which proves the option itself was understood. A made-up option produces warning BC2007 and is ignored: vbc : warning BC2007: unrecognized option '-bogusoption'; ignored. That is also why a misspelled switch in a response file does not stop a build, which is worth knowing when you read a build log.

The same options with a trailing + or - (-deterministic+, -deterministic-, -optimize-, -highentropyva-, -utf8output-, -delaysign-, -publicsign-, -skipanalyzers-, -parallel-, -doc-, -removeintchecks-, -optionexplicit+, -debug-) were all accepted, including forms the help text shows without a suffix. And -define:A=1,B was accepted (a symbol without a value is True), while ; as a separator belongs to the MSBuild property, not to the command-line option, as the DefineConstants experiment showed.

Running vbc by hand

Nothing prevents compiling without MSBuild; you need the reference assemblies and the right standard-library options because vbc on .NET does not find them itself. The project below is one source file, a response file with the options and a response file listing the 167 reference assemblies (made with ls $REF/*.dll | sed 's|^|-reference:|' > refs.rsp, where REF is the microsoft.netcore.app.ref folder .../ref/net10.0 of the reference pack):

Option Strict On

Public Module Hello

    Public Sub Main()
        Console.WriteLine("Hello from vbc " & Left("compiled by hand", 11))
    End Sub

End Module
# build.rsp
-nologo
-noconfig
-nostdlib
-nosdkpath
-target:exe
-out:Hello.dll
-optionstrict+
-rootnamespace:Hand
-define:_MyType="Empty"
-imports:System,Microsoft.VisualBasic
-vbruntime:<ref>/Microsoft.VisualBasic.dll
@refs.rsp
Hello.vb
dotnet /usr/share/dotnet/sdk/10.0.402/Roslyn/bincore/vbc.dll @build.rsp
vbc : warning BC2025: ignoring /noconfig option because it was specified in a response file
vbc exit code: 0

The Hello.runtimeconfig.json that dotnet needs to run a framework-dependent program (the SDK writes it for you in a project build) is three lines of JSON that name the framework Microsoft.NETCore.App version 10.0.0; with it, dotnet Hello.dll printed:

Hello from vbc compiled by

Notes from the run: -noconfig must be on the real command line (BC2025 otherwise, a warning only); without -define:_MyType="Empty" the compiler generates its default My classes and reports BC30002 for the Windows-only types they use (Type 'Global.Microsoft.VisualBasic.ApplicationServices.ApplicationBase' is not defined.), and the line is how the SDK stops that; and a response file is simply the options, one per line, expanded in place, which is how MSBuild itself invokes the compiler. Built and run: 1 program.

Source: Visual Basic command-line compiler, Response files, Sample compilation command lines

Visual Studio project properties

Visual Studio is a front end for the same project file: every setting it shows is an MSBuild property, and saving the page edits the .vbproj. For an SDK-style project, double-clicking the project in Solution Explorer (or the Edit Project File command) opens the XML directly, which is the quickest way to see what a page really stores. No IDE was available for the tests behind this page, so the table below takes the page and setting names from the Learn "Project Designer" pages for Visual Basic and the property names from the verified sections above; check the page layout against your Visual Studio version (the two Learn pages state that they apply to Visual Studio 2017, and the project designer has been redone since).

Settings files generate My.Settings code; see The My Namespace.

New projects start from the defaults of Tools > Options > Projects and Solutions > VB Defaults, which is why a project created in Visual Studio can have OptionStrict On while one created with dotnet new has Off: the IDE writes the option into the new project, and the SDK default is only the fallback. The debugger, Edit and Continue and Hot Reload are on Debugging and Diagnostics.

Legacy (non-SDK) project files

Until .NET Core, every Visual Basic project used a verbose format that listed everything by hand. You meet it in .NET Framework solutions, in older repositories and in the books that predate the SDK. The sample below is a typical project of that kind for a console application (legacy format, shown for recognition; not built here).

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<Project ToolsVersion="15.0" xmlns="http://schemas.microsoft.com/developer/msbuild/2003">
  <Import Project="$(MSBuildExtensionsPath)\$(MSBuildToolsVersion)\Microsoft.Common.props"
          Condition="Exists('$(MSBuildExtensionsPath)\$(MSBuildToolsVersion)\Microsoft.Common.props')" />
  <PropertyGroup>
    <Configuration Condition=" '$(Configuration)' == '' ">Debug</Configuration>
    <Platform Condition=" '$(Platform)' == '' ">AnyCPU</Platform>
    <ProjectGuid>{00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000}</ProjectGuid>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <StartupObject>Shelf.Cli.Program</StartupObject>
    <RootNamespace>Shelf.Cli</RootNamespace>
    <AssemblyName>Shelf.Cli</AssemblyName>
    <FileAlignment>512</FileAlignment>
    <MyType>Console</MyType>
    <TargetFrameworkVersion>v4.8</TargetFrameworkVersion>
    <OptionExplicit>On</OptionExplicit>
    <OptionCompare>Binary</OptionCompare>
    <OptionStrict>Off</OptionStrict>
    <OptionInfer>On</OptionInfer>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <PropertyGroup Condition=" '$(Configuration)|$(Platform)' == 'Debug|AnyCPU' ">
    <DebugSymbols>true</DebugSymbols>
    <DebugType>full</DebugType>
    <DefineDebug>true</DefineDebug>
    <DefineTrace>true</DefineTrace>
    <OutputPath>bin\Debug\</OutputPath>
    <NoWarn>42016,41999,42017,42018,42019,42032,42036,42020,42021,42022</NoWarn>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <Reference Include="System" />
    <Reference Include="System.Core" />
    <Reference Include="System.Data" />
    <Reference Include="System.Xml.Linq" />
  </ItemGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <Import Include="Microsoft.VisualBasic" />
    <Import Include="System" />
    <Import Include="System.Collections.Generic" />
    <Import Include="System.Linq" />
  </ItemGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <Compile Include="Program.vb" />
    <Compile Include="My Project\AssemblyInfo.vb" />
    <Compile Include="My Project\Application.Designer.vb">
      <AutoGen>True</AutoGen>
      <DependentUpon>Application.myapp</DependentUpon>
    </Compile>
  </ItemGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <None Include="App.config" />
    <None Include="My Project\Application.myapp">
      <Generator>MyApplicationCodeGenerator</Generator>
      <LastGenOutput>Application.Designer.vb</LastGenOutput>
    </None>
  </ItemGroup>
  <Import Project="$(MSBuildToolsPath)\Microsoft.VisualBasic.targets" />
</Project>

What the SDK-style project made redundant:

Legacy construct SDK-style replacement

ToolsVersion, the xmlns, the Microsoft.Common.props and Microsoft.VisualBasic.targets imports

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

ProjectGuid, default Configuration and Platform

Not needed (the solution file still carries project ids)

TargetFrameworkVersion v4.8

TargetFramework net48 or net481; the same project file can then move to net10.0

One PropertyGroup per configuration with DefineDebug, DefineTrace, OutputPath, NoWarn

The SDK defaults (the same NoWarn list as above) and Condition="'$(Configuration)' == 'Release'" groups only for real differences

A Compile Include for every file

The **/*.vb glob (NETSDK1022 if you keep the list)

Reference Include="System" and HintPath into a packages folder with packages.config

Implicit framework references and PackageReference

Import Include items for the default namespaces

The SDK’s implicit imports (keep only your own)

My Project\AssemblyInfo.vb

Generated from Version, Company and so on; keeping the old file with GenerateAssemblyInfo true produces duplicate-attribute errors (BC30663), so either delete the file or set GenerateAssemblyInfo to false

My Project\Application.myapp and Application.Designer.vb

Still used by Windows Forms projects that use the application framework; Console and library projects need only MyType

Settings.settings, Resources.resx

Unchanged in structure; they stay None / EmbeddedResource items

Almost every property name is the same in both formats (OutputType, RootNamespace, OptionStrict, MyType, DefineConstants), which is why a conversion is mostly deletion. A reasonable order is: create an SDK-style project that targets the same .NET Framework version (net48, net481: it compiles anywhere with the reference assemblies package, as the multi-targeting example showed), delete the lists the SDK now provides, replace packages.config with PackageReference, fix the AssemblyInfo duplicates, get the build green on the old framework, and only then change the target to net10.0 and deal with the APIs that moved. Microsoft’s Upgrade Assistant and the app-modernization tooling can automate part of this; their current capabilities were not tested for this page. Web Forms and ASP.NET MVC projects are .NET Framework projects, normally in the legacy format, as described in Web, HTTP and Services. The strategy side is on Migrating Legacy Visual Basic.

All of them

Compared with .NET Framework. An SDK-style project can target net48 or net481 and keep MyType Windows / WindowsForms, System.Data in the default imports, /subsystemversion:6.00 and the Framework’s own Microsoft.VisualBasic.dll; a project on net10.0 gets _MyType="Empty" until the template sets another value, eight default imports and the reference pack’s runtime.

Where the books and the older documentation are outdated

The books that predate the SDK-style format describe Visual Basic through a .NET Framework console template and a Visual Studio of that time; on current tooling the same programs are created with dotnet new console -lang VB or File > New in Visual Studio 2026 and build against .NET 10 (see Getting Started). Beyond the books, a few official pages lag behind the product, and a reader following them gets a wrong picture:

  • The Learn pages -langversion and Select the Visual Basic language version list LangVersion values only up to 16.9 (the compiler also accepts 17.13), and the first says the option can be set only on the command line, which is not true for a project.

  • The Learn Vbc task page lists 53 parameters, 50 of them still current; the targets pass 90.

  • The Learn MSBuild properties for Microsoft.NET.Sdk page does not mention the Visual Basic-specific properties (OptionStrict, OptionExplicit, OptionInfer, OptionCompare, RemoveIntegerChecks, MyType, VBRuntime, RootNamespace, StartupObject and DefineConstants each had zero matches in the page), so this page’s tables come from the SDK files themselves.

  • The Learn compiler-option pages do not cover everything vbc -help prints; the options -analyzer, -additionalfile, -checksumalgorithm, -errorlog, -ruleset, -reportanalyzer, -skipanalyzers, -instrument, -sourcelink, -publicsign, -generatedfilesout, -parallel, -preferreduilang, -nosdkpath, -reportivts and -version have no page named after them.

  • The Learn Compile Page and Application Page of the Project Designer say they apply to Visual Studio 2017.

  • The default OptionStrict is Off in the SDK although Learn and every style guide recommend On; there is no project template that changes it.

Summary

  • A Visual Basic project is an SDK-style .vbproj; the SDK adds the sources (glob), the references, eight global imports, the option defaults and a NoWarn list.

  • Properties become vbc options through the Vbc task (90 parameters). dotnet msbuild -getTargetResult:CoreCompile with ProvideCommandLineArgs shows the result without compiling.

  • OptionStrict Off is passed as /optionstrict:custom and relies on the default NoWarn; write $(NoWarn);..., or better set OptionStrict On in Directory.Build.props.

  • DefineConstants is comma separated; DefineDebug false does not remove DEBUG; Import items replace ImplicitUsings; Nullable and Using are inert.

  • LangVersion accepts 9 to 16.9, 17.13, default and latest; the syntax gates are those of the language history, and no syntax has been added since 15.5.

  • MyType, VBRuntime and UseReferencedVBRuntime choose the My classes and the runtime; they differ for net10.0, net10.0-windows, net481 and netstandard2.0.

  • Share settings with Directory.Build.props, Directory.Packages.props and global.json; a command-line -p: property wins over all of them.

  • dotnet new -lang VB, sln, add, build, run, test, pack, publish and format are the day-to-day commands; dotnet msbuild -pp shows the expanded project.
